title: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370
wiki_lead:
Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370 / MAS370) was an international passenger flight from Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia to Beijing Capital International Airport in China. On 8 March 2014, the Boeing 777 operating on the route disappeared from radar with 227 passengers and 12 crew members on board. Although the cause of its disapperance has been inconclusive, the aircraft was diverted manually but it is unknown who was responsible or why. It is widely regarded as the greatest mystery in aviation history.
The crew of the aircraft last communicated with air traffic control (ATC) around 38 minutes after takeoff while flying over the South China Sea. The aircraft was lost from ATC's secondary surveillance radar screens minutes later, but was tracked by the Malaysian military's primary radar system for another hour as it manually deviated westward from its planned flight path. It left radar range 200 nautical miles (370 km; 230 mi) west-northwest of Penang Island in northwestern Peninsular Malaysia.
Relying mostly on the analysis of data from the Inmarsat satellite with which the aircraft last communicated, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) initially proposed that a hypoxia event was the most likely cause given the available evidence, although no consensus has been reached among investigators concerning this theory. At various stages of the investigation, possible hijacking scenarios were considered, including crew involvement, and suspicion of the aircraft's cargo manifest. Many disappearance theories regarding the flight have also been reported by the media.
With all 227 passengers and 12 crew aboard presumed dead, the disappearance of Flight 370 was the deadliest incident involving a Boeing 777, the deadliest of 2014, and the deadliest in Malaysia Airlines' history until it was surpassed in all three regards by Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 on 17 July 2014. 
The search for the missing aircraft became the most expensive search in aviation history at US$135–160 million. It focused initially on the South China Sea and Andaman Sea, before a novel analysis of the aircraft's automated communications with an Inmarsat satellite indicated that the aircraft had travelled far southward over the southern Indian Ocean. Several pieces of debris washed ashore in the western Indian Ocean during 2015 and 2016; many of these were confirmed to have originated from Flight 370. After a three-year search across 120,000 km2 (46,000 sq mi) of ocean failed to locate the aircraft, the Joint Agency Coordination Centre heading the operation suspended its activities in January 2017. A second search launched in January 2018 by private contractor Ocean Infinity also ended without success after six months. The Malaysian Ministry of Transport's final report from July 2018 was inconclusive.
In the absence of a definitive cause of disappearance, air transport industry safety recommendations and regulations citing Flight 370 have been implemented to prevent a repetition of the circumstances associated with the loss. These include increased battery life on underwater locator beacons, lengthening of recording times on flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders, and new standards for aircraft position reporting over open ocean.
wiki_fulltext:
Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370 / MAS370) was an international passenger flight from Kuala Lumpur International Airport in Malaysia to Beijing Capital International Airport in China. On 8 March 2014, the Boeing 777 operating on the route disappeared from radar with 227 passengers and 12 crew members on board. Although the cause of its disapperance has been inconclusive, the aircraft was diverted manually but it is unknown who was responsible or why. It is widely regarded as the greatest mystery in aviation history.
The crew of the aircraft last communicated with air traffic control (ATC) around 38 minutes after takeoff while flying over the South China Sea. The aircraft was lost from ATC's secondary surveillance radar screens minutes later, but was tracked by the Malaysian military's primary radar system for another hour as it manually deviated westward from its planned flight path. It left radar range 200 nautical miles (370 km; 230 mi) west-northwest of Penang Island in northwestern Peninsular Malaysia.
Relying mostly on the analysis of data from the Inmarsat satellite with which the aircraft last communicated, the Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) initially proposed that a hypoxia event was the most likely cause given the available evidence, although no consensus has been reached among investigators concerning this theory. At various stages of the investigation, possible hijacking scenarios were considered, including crew involvement, and suspicion of the aircraft's cargo manifest. Many disappearance theories regarding the flight have also been reported by the media.
With all 227 passengers and 12 crew aboard presumed dead, the disappearance of Flight 370 was the deadliest incident involving a Boeing 777, the deadliest of 2014, and the deadliest in Malaysia Airlines' history until it was surpassed in all three regards by Malaysia Airlines Flight 17 on 17 July 2014. 
The search for the missing aircraft became the most expensive search in aviation history at US$135–160 million. It focused initially on the South China Sea and Andaman Sea, before a novel analysis of the aircraft's automated communications with an Inmarsat satellite indicated that the aircraft had travelled far southward over the southern Indian Ocean. Several pieces of debris washed ashore in the western Indian Ocean during 2015 and 2016; many of these were confirmed to have originated from Flight 370. After a three-year search across 120,000 km2 (46,000 sq mi) of ocean failed to locate the aircraft, the Joint Agency Coordination Centre heading the operation suspended its activities in January 2017. A second search launched in January 2018 by private contractor Ocean Infinity also ended without success after six months. The Malaysian Ministry of Transport's final report from July 2018 was inconclusive.
In the absence of a definitive cause of disappearance, air transport industry safety recommendations and regulations citing Flight 370 have been implemented to prevent a repetition of the circumstances associated with the loss. These include increased battery life on underwater locator beacons, lengthening of recording times on flight data recorders and cockpit voice recorders, and new standards for aircraft position reporting over open ocean.


Background


Aircraft
Flight 370 was operated by a Boeing 777-2H6ER, serial number 28420, registered as 9M-MRO. The aircraft was delivered new to Malaysia Airlines on 31 May 2002. It was powered by two Rolls-Royce Trent 892 engines and configured to carry 282 passengers in total capacity. It had accumulated 53,471.6 hours and 7,526 cycles (takeoffs and landings) in service and had not previously been involved in any major incidents, though a minor incident while taxiing at Shanghai Pudong International Airport in August 2012 resulted in a broken wing tip. Its last maintenance "A check" was carried out on 23 February 2014. The aircraft was in compliance with all applicable airworthiness directives for the airframe and engines. A replenishment of the crew member oxygen system was performed on 7 March 2014, a routine maintenance task; an examination of this procedure found nothing unusual. In a 2024 story published without attribution or information about the source, The Standard reported that ten years after MH370's disappearance, "leaked documents" show that MH370 was given supplemental fuel and crew member oxygen supplies just before takeoff. Passenger oxygen systems can generate about 12 to 15 minutes of supplemental oxygen. Crew oxygen is a separate system and allow for several hours of use. 
The Boeing 777 was introduced in 1994 and has an excellent safety record. Since its first commercial flight in June 1995, the type has suffered only six other hull losses.


Passengers and crew

The aircraft was carrying 12 Malaysian crew members and 227 passengers from 14 different nations. On the day of the disappearance, Malaysia Airlines released the names and nationalities of the passengers and crew, based on the flight manifest. The passenger list was later modified to include two Iranian passengers travelling on stolen passports.


Crew
All 12 crew members—two pilots and 10 cabin crew—were Malaysian citizens.

The pilot in command was 52-year-old Captain Zaharie Ahmad Shah from Penang. He joined Malaysia Airlines as a cadet pilot in 1981, and after training and receiving his commercial pilot's license, he became a second officer with the airline in 1983. He was promoted to captain of  the Boeing 737-400 in 1991, captain of the Airbus A330-300 in 1996, and captain of the Boeing 777-200 in 1998. He had been a type-rating instructor and a type-rating examiner since 2007. Zaharie had a total of 18,365 hours of flying experience.
The co-pilot was 26-year-old First Officer Fariq Abdul Hamid. He joined Malaysia Airlines as a cadet pilot in 2007; after becoming a second officer of the Boeing 737–400, he was promoted to first officer of the Boeing 737–400 in 2010 and then transitioned to the Airbus A330-300 in 2012. In November 2013, he began training as first officer of the Boeing 777–200 aircraft. Flight 370 was his final training flight, and he was scheduled to be examined on his next flight. Fariq had accumulated 2,763 hours of flying experience.


Passengers
Of the 227 passengers, 153 were Chinese citizens, including a group of 19 artists with six family members and four staff returning from a calligraphy exhibition of their work in Kuala Lumpur. 38 passengers were Malaysian. The remaining passengers were from 12 different countries. Twenty passengers, 12 of whom were from Malaysia and eight from China, were employees of Freescale Semiconductor.


Flight

Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370/MAS370) was an International passenger flight that departed Kuala Lumpur International Airport at 00:42 (UTC+08:00) on 8 March 2014, heading to Beijing Capital International Airport, carrying 227 passengers and 12 crew members. The aircraft climbed to its assigned cruising altitude of approximately 35,000 feet (10,700 m) and proceeded towards the waypoint IGARI over the South China Sea.
At 01:19:30, the crew acknowledged instructions to contact air traffic controllers in Ho Chi Minh City with the words, "Good night Malaysian Three Seven Zero." The crew did not establish radio contact with Ho Chi Minh controllers. This was the last recorded radio transmission from the aircraft. At 01:21:13, shortly passing IGARI, the aircraft disappeared from secondary surveillance radar—which relies on signals from the aircraft's transponder—and was manually flown through a sharp sustained left turn lasting approximately 2 minutes and 10 seconds. Investigators concluded that the turn was performed with the autopilot off, as simulator trials could not recreate the manoeuvre within that time using autopilot. 

Malaysian military primary radar continued to track the aircraft as it turned back across the Malay Peninsula, passed south of Penang Island and headed northwest along the Strait of Malacca. The final military radar detection was at 02:22:12, beyond waypoint MEKAR. The military identified the aircraft as friendly and did not intercept it.
At 01:38, Ho Chi Minh controllers contacted Kuala Lumpur to report that they had not established communication with Flight 370. Later enquiries were complicated by information from Malaysia Airlines placing the aircraft in Cambodian airspace. At 03:30, the airline explained that its reported positions were projections rather than confirmed locations. Kuala Lumpur's Aeronautical Rescue Coordination Centre was activated at 05:30, while the aircraft was still airborne.
At 07:24, Malaysia Airlines announced that contact with Flight 370 had been lost and that search-and-rescue operations had begun. Its initial statement initially gave the time of lost contact as 02:40; this was later corrected to 01:21. Unknown to anyone, the aircraft was still airborne over the Indian Ocean while the search was ongoing in the South China Sea.
On 24 March, Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak announced that satellite analysis placed the flight's end in the southern Indian Ocean. Although radio contact was not restored, the aircraft's satellite communications system logged on to the Inmarsat network at 02:25. It subsequently exchanged automated signals with a ground station and received two unanswered calls to the cockpit. Its last transmission was recorded at 08:19:37; it did not respond to further contact attempts beginning at 09:15.

On 29 January 2015, Malaysia formally declared the disappearance an accident under annexes 12 and 13 of the Chicago Convention and stated that all 239 people aboard were presumed dead.


Search

The multinational search immediately focused on the South China Sea and Strait of Malacca, while the aircraft was still airborne over the Indian Ocean. Analysis of the aircraft's satellite communications shifted the search to the southern Indian Ocean, where Australia assumed responsibility at Malaysia's request on 17 March 2014. Searches by aircraft and ships, followed by attempts to detect the underwater locator beacons attached to the flight recorders, found no wreckage or signals attributable to Flight 370.
An underwater search led by the Australian Transport Safety Bureau, with support from Malaysia and China, surveyed more than 120,000 km2 (46,000 sq mi) of seabed. The three governments suspended it on 17 January 2017 after the aircraft was not found. In January 2018, Ocean Infinity began another search on a "no find, no fee" basis, which also ended without locating the aircraft.
Ocean Infinity resumed searching in February 2025, with a new agreement covering 15,000 km2 (5,800 sq mi) of the southern Indian Ocean on a "no find, no fee" basis. After a seasonal suspension, operations resumed in December but ended on 23 January 2026 without locating the aircraft. On 29 June 2026, Malaysia announced that the agreement had been extended until 30 June 2027 to allow the remaining search area to be surveyed.


Marine debris

On 29 July 2015, more than sixteen months after the disappearance, a right flaperon was found washed ashore on Réunion, a French island in the western Indian Ocean. It was transported to Toulouse for examination by French investigators. Although its identification plate was missing, numbers on its internal components were traced to manufacturing records, confirming that it belonged to 9M-MRO. It was the first recovered wreckage positively identified as coming from Flight 370.
Further aircraft debris was recovered from beaches off the coasts of Mozambique, South Africa, Mauritius, Tanzania and Madagascar. Two pieces found in Mozambique in December 2015 and February 2016 were identified as a flap support fairing and a horizontal stabiliser panel. grok_lead: Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 (MH370) was a Boeing 777-200ER scheduled to carry 227 passengers and 12 crew from Kuala Lumpur International Airport to Beijing Capital International Airport when it disappeared on 8 March 2014 shortly after takeoff at 00:41 MYT. The aircraft lost contact with air traffic control over the South China Sea near waypoint IGARI, after which its transponder was disabled and it deviated sharply from its planned northeast route, turning back westward across the Malay Peninsula as tracked by Malaysian military primary radar. Subsequent analysis of automated satellite "handshake" pings from Inmarsat indicated the plane continued flying for about seven hours, arcing southward into the remote southeastern Indian Ocean where it likely exhausted its fuel and crashed, based on Doppler shift and elapsed time calculations validated against known flight paths. An extensive multinational search, led initially by Malaysia and later focused in the Indian Ocean by Australia, scanned more than 230,000 square kilometers of seabed using sonar and submersibles (with the total underwater search area approaching 250,000 square kilometers by 2026) but yielded no main wreckage or flight recorders, hampered by the vast, deep terrain and imprecise endpoint estimates from the satellite data. The most recent Ocean Infinity campaign, conducted in two phases from March 2025 to January 2026 and covering approximately 7,571 square kilometers of a planned 15,000-square-kilometer area, found no confirmed wreckage. Several pieces of debris, including a confirmed flaperon from the right wing found on RÃ©union Island in 2015 and two other wing fragments positively identified as from MH370, along with additional fragments assessed as almost certainly matching via serial numbers and barnacle analysis, drifted ashore on African and Indian Ocean coasts, consistent with ocean currents from a southern crash site but providing limited causal insight. The official Malaysian investigation concluded the deviations required manual intervention inconsistent with autopilot modes, ruling out mechanical failure or fire as primary causes, yet could not identify perpetrators or motives amid conflicting theories ranging from pilot action to external interference, underscoring gaps in aviation tracking and response protocols.
